item.title: Optical control stabilizes cold-atom comagnetometry
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02043-6 The use of tailored laser fields improves the coherence times of two co-trapped ytterbium isotopes, resulting in the rejection of magnetic-field noise by more than thirty-thousand-fold, opening the way to improved comagnetometry.

item.title: Measuring hard X-ray attosecond pulses
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02037-4 The generation and characterization of high-power X-ray attosecond pulses is a challenging research frontier in free-electron laser science. Now, researchers at the Linac Coherent Light Source have demonstrated experimental confirmation and measurement of hard X-ray pulses reaching 100-attosecond durations.

item.title: Theoretical method uses light to locate anyons, potential quantum computing building blocks
item.description: Theoretical physicists at Emory University have discovered a way to use light to detect the "spectral fingerprints" of anyons—exotic quasiparticles that emerge from the collective behavior of many electrons. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters. The work offers a new tool for the study of anyons, which hold potential as fundamental building blocks for quantum computing.

item.title: Quantum skyrmions outlast entanglement, hinting at more resilient networks
item.description: Quantum networks could one day connect quantum computers into more powerful systems and enable new forms of secure communication. But a fundamental obstacle stands in the way: Quantum information is extraordinarily fragile, and the entanglement between particles of light on which such networks would depend is easily disrupted.

item.description: Graphene, a material consisting of a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern, has proved promising for various technological applications. Materials in which several layers of graphene are stacked together can exhibit different advantageous properties.

item.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
item.description: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

item.title: Quantum gates set speed record at 6.8 nanoseconds with over 99.98% accuracy
item.description: Researchers from Jülich, Aachen and Cologne have performed a quantum operation on a qubit in just 6.8 nanoseconds—with more than 99.98% accuracy. Such operations typically take several tens of nanoseconds in superconducting quantum computers. The paper was published in Nature Communications.

item.title: New converter could bridge light wavelength gap in quantum communications
item.description: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices using quantum mechanical effects, could potentially allow users to share information more securely and efficiently. Building these networks typically entails linking stationary qubits, units of quantum information encoded in trapped ions or other physical systems, using photons (particles of light) transmitted through optical fibers.
